rewritten_text: Then Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights belonging to the castle, met Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay. The four charged fiercely together, shattering their spears down to their hands. Next Sir Pertolope rode out from the castle against Sir Lionel, and the green knight Pertolope struck down Lionel, Sir Launcelot’s brother. Noble heralds observed all these deeds, recording who acquitted himself best and noting their names. Sir Bleobaris then broke his spear against Sir Gareth, but the stroke sent Bleobaris himself to the ground. Seeing this, Sir Galihodin called upon Gareth to defend himself, and Gareth likewise struck him down. Sir Galihud took a spear to avenge his brother and received the same treatment. So too did Sir Dinadan and his brother La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore le Disirous, and Sir Dodinas le Savage: Gareth overthrew them all with a single spear. King Aswisance of Ireland, watching these exploits, wondered who the knight could be, for at one moment he appeared green, and on his next return blue. With every course he rode, back and forth, his colour changed, so that neither king nor knight could readily recognize him. Then Sir Agwisance, King of Ireland, charged against Gareth, who hurled him from his horse, saddle and all. King Carados of Scotland came next, and Gareth cast down both horse and rider. He served King Uriens of Gore in just the same fashion. Sir Bagdemagus then entered, and he and his horse were brought to earth as well. Bagdemagus’s son Meliganus broke a spear upon Gareth with mighty, knightly force. At this, the noble prince Sir Galahault cried aloud, “Knight of many colours, thou hast jousted well. Prepare now, that I may joust with thee.” Hearing him, Gareth took up a great spear, and they rode together. The prince’s spear broke, but Gareth struck the left side of his helmet so hard that he swayed this way and that, and would have fallen had his men not supported him. “Truly,” King Arthur said, “this knight of many colours is a worthy knight.” He therefore summoned Sir Launcelot and asked him to meet the stranger. “Sir,” Launcelot answered, “I am willing to spare him for the present, for he has laboured sufficiently today. When a good knight performs so well, it ill becomes another good knight to rob him of his glory, particularly after seeing him endure such exertion. Perhaps,” he continued, “he has a special cause here today, and perhaps this lady loves him best of all those present. I plainly see how he strives and forces himself to accomplish great deeds. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, he shall have today’s honour. Even were it within my power to deprive him of it, I would not.”

On the morning fixed for Admiral and Mrs Croft’s visit to Kellynch Hall, Anne found nothing more natural than taking her customary walk to Lady Russell’s and remaining absent until the affair was concluded; after which, she found it equally natural to regret having lost the chance of meeting them.

The encounter gave great satisfaction to both parties and settled the business immediately. Each lady had already inclined towards agreement and consequently perceived only good breeding in the other. Among the gentlemen, the Admiral displayed such hearty cheerfulness and such frank, confiding generosity that Sir Walter could not remain untouched. Mr Shepherd had, moreover, flattered him into his most polished behaviour by declaring that the Admiral knew him by reputation as a pattern of fine manners.

House, grounds, and furniture were approved; the Crofts were approved; terms and dates, everybody and everything, were satisfactory. Mr Shepherd’s clerks began their labours without one preliminary disagreement requiring alteration in any part of what “This indenture sheweth.”

Sir Walter promptly pronounced the Admiral the handsomest sailor he had ever encountered. He even ventured that, were his own man allowed to arrange the Admiral’s hair, he should feel no shame in appearing with him anywhere. With answering cordiality, the Admiral remarked to his wife as their carriage passed back through the park, “I thought we should soon strike a bargain, my dear, notwithstanding what we heard at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames alight, but I see no harm in him.” These reciprocal tributes might fairly have been judged of equal value.

The Crofts would enter at Michaelmas; and since Sir Walter intended to depart for Bath during the preceding month, every connected arrangement demanded prompt attention.

Lady Russell was persuaded that Anne would be granted neither usefulness nor consequence in selecting their intended house. She disliked seeing her hurried away so early and hoped to enable her to remain until she could herself convey her to Bath after Christmas. Her own engagements, however, would take her away from Kellynch for several weeks, making the full invitation she desired impossible. Anne dreaded the possible September heat amid the white brilliance of Bath, and mourned the loss of those country autumn months whose influence was at once so tender and so melancholy. Yet, when all circumstances were weighed, she did not believe she wished to stay.

The witness could not be certain whether the voice belonged to a man or a woman. He could not understand the words but thought the language was Spanish. His description of the room and bodies agreed with the account we published yesterday.

“Henri Duval, a neighbor and silversmith, states that he belonged to the first group entering the house. His testimony generally supports Musèt’s. After forcing their way in, they shut the door again to exclude the crowd, which was gathering rapidly despite the late hour. He believes the high-pitched voice was Italian and is certain it was not French. He cannot say whether it was a man’s voice; it might have been a woman’s. He does not know Italian and could distinguish no words, but the intonation convinced him that the speaker was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter and had spoken with both often. He is sure the voice belonged to neither victim.

“—— Odenheimer, restaurant owner, offered his evidence voluntarily. He is from Amsterdam and speaks no French, so he was questioned through an interpreter. He was passing the house when the screams occurred. They continued for several minutes, perhaps ten, and were long, loud, and extremely frightening and distressing. He was among those who entered. He confirmed the earlier evidence in every detail except one. He was certain the high-pitched voice belonged to a man, specifically a Frenchman. He could not make out the words. They were loud, rapid, and uneven, apparently expressing fear as well as anger. The voice was harsh, rather than truly high-pitched; he would not describe it as shrill. The gruff voice repeatedly said ‘sacré’ and ‘diable,’ and once ‘mon Dieu.’

“Jules Mignaud, banker with Mignaud et Fils of Rue Deloraine, is the elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye owned some property. She opened an account at his bank in the spring eight years earlier and frequently deposited small amounts. She made no withdrawal until three days before her death, when she personally withdrew four thousand francs. She received the money in gold, and a clerk accompanied it home.

“Adolphe Le Bon, a clerk at Mignaud et Fils, states that around noon that day he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye home with the four thousand francs in two bags. When the door opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one bag from him, while the older woman took the other.
